title: Where Does Northern B.C. Begin?
summary: Prince George feels northern. Williams Lake often does too. But official maps draw the line in different places, because each boundary was built to answer a different question.
sourceNote: This story uses repository snapshots from the B.C. Ministry of Health, B.C. Energy Regulator, Statistics Canada, and B.C. natural-resource administration. These are administrative and statistical definitions — not a survey of how people describe where they live.
details: Northern B.C. looks obvious until a boundary has to be drawn. Health services, energy regulation, census geography, and natural-resource administration divide the same province for different purposes.

The story is intentionally encoded as data. Its cards declare a camera position, a visible layer set, feature highlights, and place markers; the reusable story-map workspace turns those declarations into a scrolling map narrative.
Local repository paths can be replaced with HTTPS GeoJSON URLs in another project package, provided the remote host permits browser access.

scenes.label: The question
scenes.title: A line everyone knows — until they try to draw it
scenes.text: Ask where Northern B.C. begins and Prince George is an easy answer. Williams Lake is harder. Rather than picking one true north, this story compares the boundaries institutions actually use, and asks what each was built to do.

scenes.label: Prince George
scenes.title: Prince George is northern in the health system
scenes.text: Prince George sits inside Northern Health, the largest of the five health authorities by area. Here the everyday description and the service-delivery boundary agree: the city is clearly on the northern side of the institutional line.

callout.label: Health Authority
callout.detail: One of five authorities; covers roughly two-thirds of B.C.'s land area.

scenes.label: Williams Lake
scenes.title: Williams Lake lands on the other side
scenes.text: Williams Lake sits in Interior Health, not far from the Northern Health boundary. Many people there describe themselves as living in the north. Regional identity does not stop cleanly at a service boundary, so this map can feel at odds with how the Cariboo talks about itself.

callout.label: Health Authority
callout.detail: Williams Lake is inside Interior Health, about 240 km south of Prince George.

scenes.label: Four levels
scenes.title: Health boundaries zoom from province to community
scenes.text: B.C.'s health geography nests four levels: Health Authority, Health Service Delivery Area, Local Health Area, and Community Health Service Area. Turning them on together shows a broad service region resolving into local planning units — the same territory, described at four different resolutions.

callout.label: Nesting
callout.detail: Health Authorities, HSDAs, Local Health Areas, then Community Health Service Areas.

scenes.label: Energy
scenes.title: For energy regulation, Prince George is southwest
scenes.text: The B.C. Energy Regulator divides its operating geography into North, Central, South East, and South West zones. Under that map Prince George sits in South West, and Fort St. John — far to the northeast — sits in Central. The zone names describe an agency's operating territory, not a regional identity.

callout.label: BCER zone
callout.detail: Prince George is South West here, while Fort St. John is Central.

scenes.label: Census
scenes.title: Statistics Canada draws another north–south line
scenes.text: The North/South variant of the 2021 census classification labels every census subdivision in Canada using a set of measured variables rather than a single drawn line. Clipped to B.C., it places both Prince George and Williams Lake in the North — closer to how people in the Cariboo describe themselves.

callout.label: B.C. census subdivisions
callout.detail: Both Prince George and Williams Lake are classified North.

scenes.label: Cariboo
scenes.title: The Cariboo is the gap between two answers
scenes.text: Williams Lake is the clearest example of the disagreement. The health map puts it in the Interior; the census classification puts it in the North. Neither is wrong — they were built from different inputs for different jobs, and the Cariboo happens to sit exactly where those jobs diverge.
scenes.focus: Williams Lake · North by census, Interior by health

callout.label: Same town, two answers
callout.detail: Census says North. Health says Interior Health.

scenes.label: Resources
scenes.title: Natural-resource administration redraws the province again
scenes.text: Natural Resource Regions organize field operations around areas such as Omineca, Cariboo, Skeena, and the Northeast. This map avoids a single north–south split entirely, and its outer edges track the health authority boundaries more closely than either the energy or census maps do.

callout.label: Region
callout.detail: Prince George is the Omineca region's administrative centre.

scenes.label: What gives?
scenes.title: The boundary is an argument about purpose
scenes.text: None of these maps settles where Northern B.C. truly begins. Each makes a boundary useful for health delivery, regulation, statistics, or resource administration. The better question is not only “Where is north?” but “Who drew this line, and what did they need it to do?”
